title: Precision Enhancement for Legal Discovery Systems
business: Corporate legal departments managing massive document repositories for litigation discovery.
problem: Initial keyword-based retrieval often returns large sets of documents that are topically relevant but contextually misaligned with the specific legal query, forcing attorneys to manually filter through irrelevant noise.
solution: Implementing a two-stage retrieval pipeline where a high-recall initial search retrieves a broad candidate set, followed by a BERT-based reranker that evaluates the semantic relationship between the query and each candidate document to assign a precise relevance score.
steps: Execute an initial retrieval query using traditional BM25 or vector search to fetch the top 100 candidate documents.
Pass the original user query and each candidate document text as a concatenated input pair into a pre-trained BERT model.
Compute a relevance score for each pair using the model's classification head.
Sort the candidate list in descending order based on these refined scores.
Return the top-ranked subset to the user interface for review.
outcome: Users receive a highly curated list of documents where the most contextually significant information appears at the top, significantly reducing the time spent on manual document review.
limitation: The primary limitation is computational latency; because the reranker processes every candidate document individually, it is significantly slower than the initial retrieval stage. To check for this, monitor the p99 latency of the request-response cycle as the candidate pool size increases.
